prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions (SRBMs) living in the closures of domains with piecewise smooth boundaries are of interest in applied probability because of their role as heavy traffic approximations for some stochastic networks. In this paper, assuming certain conditions on the domains and directions of reflection, a perturbation result, or invariance principle, for SRBMs is proved. This provides sufficient conditions for a process that satisfies the definition of an SRBM, except for small random perturbations in the defining conditions, to be close in distribution to an SRBM. A crucial ingredient in the proof of this result is an oscillation inequality for solutions of a perturbed Skorokhod problem. We use the invariance principle to show weak existence of SRBMs under mild conditions. We also use the invariance principle, in conjunction with known uniqueness results for SRBMs, to give some sufficient conditions for validating approximations involving (i) SRBMs in convex polyhedrons with a constant reflection vector field on each face of the polyhedron, and (ii) SRBMs in bounded domains with piecewise smooth boundaries and possibly nonconstant reflection vector fields on the boundary surfaces.

outputs.L1: Semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions (SRBMs) in the closures of domains with piecewise smooth boundaries are of interest in applied probability because they serve as heavy-traffic approximations for certain stochastic networks. In this paper, under specific conditions on the domains and reflection directions, we establish a perturbation result, or invariance principle, for SRBMs. This result provides sufficient conditions under which a process satisfying the definition of an SRBM—apart from small random perturbations in the defining conditions—is close in distribution to an SRBM. A crucial component of the proof is an oscillation inequality for solutions to a perturbed Skorokhod problem. We apply the invariance principle to establish weak existence of SRBMs under mild conditions. In conjunction with known uniqueness results for SRBMs, we also use the invariance principle to provide sufficient conditions for validating approximations involving (i) SRBMs in convex polyhedra with a constant reflection vector field on each face, and (ii) SRBMs in bounded domains with piecewise smooth boundaries and potentially nonconstant reflection vector fields on the boundary surfaces.
outputs.L2: Semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions (SRBMs) evolving in the closures of regions with piecewise smooth boundaries are important in applied probability because they serve as heavy-traffic limits for certain stochastic networks. Under specified assumptions on the geometry of the domains and the reflection directions, this paper establishes a perturbation theorem—also viewed as an invariance principle—for SRBMs. The theorem gives sufficient criteria ensuring that a process whose defining SRBM properties hold up to small random errors is close in distribution to an SRBM. A key part of the argument is an oscillation bound for solutions to a perturbed Skorokhod problem. The invariance principle is then applied to prove weak existence of SRBMs under relatively mild assumptions. Combined with established uniqueness theorems, it also yields sufficient conditions for justifying approximations involving: (i) SRBMs in convex polyhedra, where each face has a constant reflection vector field; and (ii) SRBMs in bounded, piecewise smooth domains, where reflection vector fields along the boundary surfaces may vary.

Semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions (SRBMs) provide important heavy-traffic approximations for a broad class of stochastic networks. The paper develops an invariance principle showing that stochastic processes whose defining SRBM conditions are subject to small random perturbations nevertheless converge in distribution to an SRBM. Thus, approximate models retain the limiting behavior of the ideal reflected diffusion even when their dynamics satisfy the relevant conditions only asymptotically.

A central ingredient in the proof is an oscillation inequality for solutions of a perturbed Skorokhod problem. This inequality controls fluctuations of both the constrained process and the associated regulating terms, allowing the authors to establish tightness and identify subsequential limits.

The invariance principle also yields weak existence of SRBMs under relatively mild assumptions. When combined with established uniqueness results, it provides a rigorous foundation for using SRBMs as approximations in a wide range of settings, including convex polyhedrons and bounded piecewise smooth domains, with either constant or spatially varying reflection fields.
outputs.L4:
The paper develops an invariance principle for semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions (SRBMs) in piecewise smooth domains. These processes evolve like Brownian motions in the interior of a domain but are constrained to remain in its closure by boundary reflection. At regular boundary points, the constraining force acts in a prescribed reflection direction; at nonsmooth points, several boundary faces and reflection directions may be active simultaneously. This geometry makes convergence analysis substantially more difficult than in smooth domains or orthants.

The main result gives conditions under which a sequence of constrained stochastic processes converges weakly to an SRBM. The approximating processes may contain small random perturbations and need not solve the limiting Skorokhod problem exactly. Instead, they are represented as perturbed solutions whose unconstrained components converge to Brownian motion and whose boundary terms act approximately in the appropriate reflection directions. This formulation covers many discrete-time, numerical, and queueing-network approximations.

A central ingredient is an oscillation inequality for perturbed Skorokhod problems. The inequality bounds the oscillations of both the constrained path and its regulating term in terms of the oscillation of the driving path and the size of the perturbation. Its proof uses the local geometry of the piecewise smooth boundary and compatibility conditions on the reflection field. The estimate provides the compactness needed to establish tightness and prevents small errors near intersections of boundary faces from producing uncontrolled motion.

After tightness is obtained, the paper identifies every subsequential limit. The limiting process remains in the domain, has the required Brownian drift and covariance structure in the interior, and accumulates its constraining term only on the boundary in admissible reflection directions. Thus the limit satisfies the defining submartingale or Skorokhod characterization of an SRBM. Importantly, the argument does not require uniqueness in law merely to construct a limit. It therefore also yields weak existence of SRBMs under relatively mild geometric and regularity assumptions.

When uniqueness in law is available, the identification of subsequential limits implies convergence of the entire sequence. By combining the invariance principle with existing uniqueness results, the paper validates SRBM approximations in several important settings. These include convex polyhedral domains, bounded piecewise smooth domains with constant reflection directions on each face, and bounded piecewise smooth domains with spatially varying reflection fields. The result therefore supplies a general framework for proving diffusion approximations of stochastic systems subject to state constraints, including models arising from queueing networks, heavy-traffic theory, and constrained numerical schemes.
outputs.L5:
## Semimartingales, Brownian Motion, and SRBMs

A **semimartingale** is a stochastic process that can be decomposed into the sum of a local martingale and a process of finite variation. More precisely, a process \(X\) is a semimartingale if it can be written as

\[
X(t)=X(0)+M(t)+A(t),
\]

where \(M\) is a local martingale and \(A\) is an adapted finite-variation process. Semimartingales form the natural class of integrators in Itô stochastic calculus. They include Brownian motion, Lévy processes, and solutions of many stochastic differential equations.

**Brownian motion** is one of the most important examples. A \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion \(B(t)\) has continuous paths, independent Gaussian increments, and covariance proportional to elapsed time. A Brownian motion with drift \(\mu\) and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) can be written as

\[
X(t)=X(0)+\mu t+\Sigma^{1/2}B(t).
\]

When such a process is required to remain inside a constrained domain, a regulating term must be added. This leads to **semimartingale reflected Brownian motions**, commonly abbreviated as **SRBMs**.

For example, an SRBM in the nonnegative orthant

\[
G=\mathbb{R}_+^d
\]

typically has the representation

\[
Z(t)=Z(0)+\mu t+\Sigma^{1/2}B(t)+R\,Y(t).
\]

Here:

- \(Z(t)\) is the constrained process and remains in \(G\);
- \(\mu\) is the drift vector;
- \(\Sigma\) is the covariance matrix;
- \(B(t)\) is a standard \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion;
- \(R\) is the reflection matrix;
- \(Y(t)\) is a vector of nondecreasing regulator processes.

Each component \(Y_i\) increases only when \(Z\) is on the corresponding boundary face:

\[
\int_0^\infty \mathbf{1}_{\{Z_i(t)>0\}}\,dY_i(t)=0.
\]

Thus, the regulator acts only when necessary to prevent the process from leaving the domain. If \(R\) is the identity matrix, reflection is normal to each boundary. More general matrices produce **oblique reflection**, meaning that contact with one boundary may push the process in several coordinate directions.

The construction of an SRBM is closely related to the **Skorokhod problem**. Given an unconstrained path, the Skorokhod map adds the minimal regulating term needed to keep that path inside the prescribed domain. Conditions on the geometry of the domain and the reflection directions are required to guarantee existence and uniqueness.

SRBMs are particularly important in queueing theory and stochastic networks. Under heavy-traffic scaling, queue-length or workload processes often converge to reflected Brownian motions. The reflection term represents constraints such as the impossibility of negative queue lengths, while drift and covariance encode average service behavior and random fluctuations.

The long-term behavior of an SRBM depends strongly on its drift and reflection matrix. Under suitable stability conditions, it has a stationary distribution. In special cases this distribution has a product form, but in general it is difficult to compute. Consequently, SRBMs lie at the intersection of stochastic calculus, partial differential equations, convex geometry, and applied probability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a probability theory paper proving an invariance principle for semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions in domains with piecewise smooth boundaries.
counterfactuals.output: We establish an invariance principle for semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions in domains with piecewise smooth boundaries. We consider a sequence of constrained stochastic processes whose interior dynamics satisfy a functional central limit theorem and whose boundary corrections approximate prescribed, possibly oblique, reflection fields on the smooth boundary faces. Under geometric regularity, compatibility, and nondegeneracy conditions near intersections of faces, we prove tightness in the Skorokhod space and show that every weak limit solves the corresponding reflected submartingale problem. Uniqueness in law then yields convergence to the semimartingale reflecting Brownian motion with the specified drift, covariance matrix, and reflection directions. The proof combines localization near boundary strata, estimates controlling time spent near the nonsmooth part of the boundary, and a characterization of the limiting regulator. The result applies to broad classes of discrete-time and continuous-time approximations, including constrained random walks and queueing-network models in piecewise smooth domains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a research article on perturbed Skorokhod problems and weak existence of SRBMs.
counterfactuals.output:
The article develops a stability theory for **perturbed Skorokhod problems** and uses it to prove **weak existence of semimartingale reflected Brownian motions (SRBMs)** in domains with oblique reflection.

Main results:

- **Perturbed Skorokhod formulation:** It allows small errors in the state, boundary constraints, and reflection directions. This is useful for discrete-time approximations and situations where the constraining process is not an exact solution of the Skorokhod problem.

- **Oscillation and tightness estimates:** Under suitable geometric conditions on the domain and reflection field, the authors bound the oscillations of both the constrained path and its regulator in terms of the driving path and perturbation size. These estimates yield compactness and tightness.

- **Stability under vanishing perturbations:** If the driving processes converge and the perturbations vanish, subsequential limits solve the intended Skorokhod problem. Thus approximate reflected processes can be used to construct exact ones.

- **Weak existence of SRBMs:** Applying the stability results to random-walk or Euler-type approximations, the paper proves the existence in distribution of SRBMs with specified drift, covariance, and oblique reflection directions.

- **Generality:** The framework accommodates nonsmooth, typically polyhedral, domains and multiple active boundary faces, without requiring an explicit or globally Lipschitz Skorokhod map.

Overall, the paper’s central contribution is to turn deterministic robustness results for approximate reflection problems into a probabilistic existence theorem for multidimensional SRBMs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical paper abstract explaining how an oscillation inequality yields a perturbation theorem for reflecting Brownian motions and validates stochastic-network approximations.
counterfactuals.output: We establish a perturbation theorem for reflecting Brownian motions in piecewise smooth domains using an oscillation inequality for the associated Skorokhod problem. The inequality controls the modulus of continuity of both the constrained path and its regulating process in terms of the oscillation of the driving signal, uniformly over nearby domains, reflection fields, and covariance parameters. This uniform pathwise estimate yields tightness for sequences of reflected processes and prevents boundary corrections from accumulating away from the prescribed reflection directions. Combined with continuity of the Skorokhod map and uniqueness of the limiting submartingale problem, it identifies every subsequential limit as the reflecting Brownian motion determined by the limiting geometric and stochastic data. Consequently, reflecting Brownian motions are stable under simultaneous perturbations of the domain, drift, covariance matrix, reflection directions, and initial conditions. As an application, the theorem provides a rigorous justification for diffusion approximations of stochastic networks: after heavy-traffic scaling, network state processes and their regulator processes converge jointly to the corresponding reflected Brownian model, even when the prelimit constraint sets and boundary mechanisms vary with the scaling parameter. Thus, the oscillation inequality supplies the key compactness and boundary-control estimates needed to convert local network approximations into process-level convergence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a concise academic overview of sufficient conditions under which approximate SRBMs converge weakly to true SRBMs, including applications to convex polyhedra and bounded piecewise smooth domains.
counterfactuals.output:
Let \(G\subset\mathbb R^{d}\) be a domain whose boundary is decomposed into finitely many faces \(F_i\), with prescribed inward reflection fields \(r_i(x)\). An SRBM \(Z\) in \(\bar G\) has the representation
\[
Z(t)=Z(0)+\mu t+\Sigma^{1/2}B(t)+\sum_i\int_0^t r_i(Z(s))\,dL_i(s),
\]
where each \(L_i\) is nondecreasing and increases only when \(Z\in F_i\).

A standard weak-convergence theorem applies to approximate processes \(Z^n\) provided the following hold.

1. **Convergence of the unconstrained part.**  
   The driving processes \(X^n\) converge jointly with the initial conditions to
   \[
   X(t)=Z(0)+\mu t+\Sigma^{1/2}B(t),
   \]
   usually through convergence of semimartingale characteristics or a functional central limit theorem.

2. **Asymptotically valid reflection decomposition.**  
   Up to errors vanishing uniformly on compact time intervals,
   \[
   Z^n=X^n+\sum_i\int r_i^n(Z^n)\,dL_i^n,
   \]
   where \(r_i^n\to r_i\) locally uniformly, the regulators \(L_i^n\) are asymptotically nondecreasing, and \(L_i^n\) can increase only when \(Z^n\) lies within a vanishing neighborhood of \(F_i\).

3. **State-space and jump control.**  
   The distance of \(Z^n\) from \(\bar G\), all decomposition errors, and the maximal jumps of \(Z^n,X^n,L^n\) converge to zero in probability on compact intervals.

4. **Geometric regularity and tightness.**  
   The domain and reflection cones satisfy a uniform inward-pointing or obliqueness condition, together with a local projection/oscillation property. These conditions imply \(C\)-tightness of \((Z^n,L^n)\) and prevent cancellation among reflection terms at corners.

5. **Well-posedness of the limiting problem.**  
   The reflected diffusion—equivalently, the associated submartingale problem or extended Skorokhod problem—is unique in law. Identification then shows that every subsequential limit is the desired SRBM, and hence \(Z^n\Rightarrow Z\).

At nonsmooth boundary points one additionally requires that the admissible reflection cone be the cone generated by the active face directions and that the limit spend zero Lebesgue time on exceptional boundary sets where the submartingale characterization is not directly imposed.

### Convex polyhedra

For
\[
G=\{x:\langle n_i,x\rangle\ge c_i,\ i=1,\dots,m\},
\]
with constant reflection directions \(r_i\), the geometric hypotheses reduce to finite-dimensional matrix conditions. Typical sufficient assumptions are:

- \(\langle n_i,r_i\rangle>0\);
- for every set of simultaneously active faces, the corresponding normal/reflection matrices satisfy a completely-\(\mathcal S\), coercivity, or equivalent inward-pointing condition;
- the associated Skorokhod problem is Lipschitz or at least well posed.

Under these conditions, approximate queueing-network or random-walk models whose primitive noise satisfies an FCLT and whose boundary pushes are asymptotically supported on the appropriate faces converge weakly to the polyhedral SRBM.

### Bounded piecewise smooth domains

If \(G\) is bounded and is locally an intersection of finitely many \(C^{2}\) domains, sufficient conditions include:

- continuous, uniformly oblique reflection fields on each smooth face;
- a uniform compatibility condition between active inward normals and reflection directions at edges and corners;
- existence of a locally regular projection onto \(\bar G\);
- well-posedness of the reflected-diffusion submartingale problem.

Boundedness supplies compact containment, while the projection and obliqueness estimates yield regulator tightness. Consequently, Euler schemes, penalized diffusions, and other approximate constrained processes satisfying the preceding support and error conditions converge weakly in \(D([0,\infty),\bar G)\), with continuous limits, to the true SRBM.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** Semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions (SRBMs) provide canonical diffusion approximations for constrained stochastic networks operating in heavy traffic. This article develops an invariance-principle framework in which suitably centered and scaled queue-length, workload, or storage processes converge to Brownian motions confined to a polyhedral or piecewise smooth domain by a possibly state-dependent, oblique reflection field. The analysis combines functional central limit theorems for primitive processes with continuity and stability properties of the associated Skorokhod problem. Sufficient conditions are established for existence of weak SRBM solutions, including settings in which reflection directions vary along the boundary and may be discontinuous at nonsmooth boundary intersections. Uniqueness in law is obtained through well-posedness of the corresponding submartingale problem, while stronger regularity and geometric assumptions yield pathwise uniqueness and strong existence. The results clarify how boundary geometry, covariance degeneracy, and compatibility of reflection directions govern both the validity of heavy-traffic limits and the characterization of the limiting diffusion. This framework extends classical constant-reflection invariance principles and supports diffusion approximations for networks with routing, service, or control mechanisms that induce spatially variable boundary behavior.
